## Solution

**Identifying the distribution.** The given $F(x)$ is the CDF of a (symmetric) triangular distribution on $[-a, a]$. Note that the stated middle piece $(a+x)^2/(2a^2)$ evaluated at $x=a$ gives $2\neq 1$, so the CDF must be understood in its complete form (the standard textbook statement of this example):

$$F(x)= \begin{cases}0 & x \leq -a \\ \dfrac{(a+x)^{2}}{2 a^{2}} & -a < x \leq 0 \\ 1-\dfrac{(a-x)^{2}}{2 a^{2}} & 0 < x \leq a \\ 1 & x > a\end{cases}$$

One checks consistency: $F(-a)=0$, $F(0)=\tfrac{1}{2}$, $F(a)=1$, and $F$ is continuous and non-decreasing.

**Density.** Differentiating $F$:

$$f(x)=F'(x)= \begin{cases}\dfrac{a+x}{a^{2}} & -a < x \leq 0 \\[4pt] \dfrac{a-x}{a^{2}} & 0 < x \leq a \\[4pt] 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$

This is the symmetric triangular density (peak at $0$, base on $[-a,a]$).

**Computing $\mathbb{E}[X]$.**

$$\mathbb{E}[X]=\int_{-a}^{a} x\,f(x)\,dx=\frac{1}{a^{2}}\int_{-a}^{0} x(a+x)\,dx+\frac{1}{a^{2}}\int_{0}^{a} x(a-x)\,dx.$$

*First integral:*

$$\frac{1}{a^{2}}\int_{-a}^{0}(ax+x^{2})\,dx=\frac{1}{a^{2}}\left[\frac{ax^{2}}{2}+\frac{x^{3}}{3}\right]_{-a}^{0}=\frac{1}{a^{2}}\left[0-\left(\frac{a^{3}}{2}-\frac{a^{3}}{3}\right)\right]=\frac{1}{a^{2}}\!\left(-\frac{a^{3}}{6}\right)=-\frac{a}{6}.$$

*Second integral:*

$$\frac{1}{a^{2}}\int_{0}^{a}(ax-x^{2})\,dx=\frac{1}{a^{2}}\left[\frac{ax^{2}}{2}-\frac{x^{3}}{3}\right]_{0}^{a}=\frac{1}{a^{2}}\left(\frac{a^{3}}{2}-\frac{a^{3}}{3}\right)=\frac{1}{a^{2}}\!\left(\frac{a^{3}}{6}\right)=\frac{a}{6}.$$

**Combining:**

$$\mathbb{E}[X]=-\frac{a}{6}+\frac{a}{6}=0.$$

This is consistent with the symmetry argument: $f(-x)=f(x)$, so the distribution is symmetric about $0$, hence the mean is $0$.

$$\boxed{\mathbb{E}[X]=0}$$
